analysis.one_liner: Requires food companies to report contaminated food and gives regulators power to order recalls and impose fines.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it was referred to two House committees in February 2009 and died when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal meat, poultry, and food safety laws to require anyone in the food supply chain — except household consumers — who suspects food is contaminated or mislabeled to tell the government. If the Secretary finds the food could sicken people, companies would get a first chance to pull it from shelves voluntarily; if they failed to act in time, the government could order distribution stopped and recalls carried out, with mandatory hearings on the order. The bill would also let the Agriculture Secretary refuse or withdraw federal inspection from plants with willful or repeated violations, and let regulators impose civil fines of up to $100,000 per violation (per day, for each day it continues) against companies, and up to $500,000 per act against firms under the food and drug law.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers: contaminated meat, poultry, and other food would have to be reported and pulled from the market quickly, and companies that hid problems or ignored warnings would face fines. Families would be told about recalls of food they may have bought.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Anyone who eats meat, poultry, or packaged food

how_it_helps.text: Requires anyone in the supply chain who has reason to believe meat, poultry, or other food is adulterated or misbranded to notify the Secretary of the identity and location of the product [S2][S3].

Gives the government power to require immediate cessation of distribution and order a recall if a company does not voluntarily act within the prescribed time, after a hearing held within two business days [S3].
Requires the Secretary to notify consumers who may have received the tainted product and appropriate state and local health officials [S3].

Allows the Agriculture Secretary to refuse or withdraw federal inspection from establishments with willful or repeated violations — effectively shutting a plant that cannot clean up its act — and to suspend inspection first when needed to protect consumer health [S3].

Authorizes civil penalties of up to $100,000 per violation (each day a violation continues counts separately) under the meat and poultry laws, and up to $100,000 for individuals and $500,000 for companies under the food and drug law, with the amount scaled to the size of the business and its violation history [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Meat and poultry processors, food manufacturers, distributors, and retailers would bear the cost of mandatory reporting, record-keeping, rapid recalls, and fines. Small processors would face the same obligations as large ones, though fines are scaled to business size.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on the whole supply chain, including small meat processors and distributors, for whom record-keeping, notification, and recall procedures could be a real burden even before any fine is assessed [S3].

The bill keeps recalls voluntary in the first instance: the government must give companies an opportunity to recall on their own before ordering mandatory action, which critics of that approach say delays getting contaminated food off shelves [S3].

It gives the Secretaries substantial discretion over when to order recalls and how much to fine, with judicial review limited to the record of the agency's decision — power concentrated in the department carrying out the enforcement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is direct: faster reporting, faster recalls, and consumer notice when dangerous food has been sold. The costs are compliance and recall expenses for food companies, and the bill is deliberately built so that recalls stay voluntary unless a company fails to act — a concession that softens the burden on industry but also weakens the mandate. The core trade-off is consumer protection against industry compliance cost, with modest protection for small firms built into the penalty structure.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture and Energy and Commerce committees in February 2009 and sent to their subcommittees, and neither chamber ever voted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette (D-CO), joined by Reps. Jerrold Nadler and Rosa DeLauro, introduced the bill on February 3, 2009 [S1][S3].
The bill was referred to the Agriculture Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
Within two days it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health, and in April to the Agriculture Subcommittee on Livestock, Dairy, and Poultry [S5].
Thirteen House Democrats cosponsored it; no further action of any kind was taken, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote in either chamber [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Meat and poultry processors and food companies that would have faced mandatory reporting, recall orders, withdrawal of inspection, and civil fines are better off because the bill never advanced; consumers got no new federal recall powers from this bill during that Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Meat and food companies that faced fines

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill's support was all Democratic (all 13 cosponsors) and its death occurred in committee without a recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would subject them to mandatory contamination reporting, possible withdrawal of federal inspection — which halts legal sales — and fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. Those enforcement powers exist to keep contaminated meat off store shelves, so the industry's interest runs against the consumer's here.

They would face mandatory notification when they suspect food may sicken people, government-ordered recall authority after a two-day hearing, and civil fines up to $500,000 per act. The cost is real, but it is the cost of removing dangerous products from stores quickly.

Retailers are among the 'appropriate persons' who must cease distribution and can be penalized for food sold on their shelves. They benefit alongside consumers from quicker recalls that limit the damage of an outbreak traced to their stores.
